sermons.life_context: A resident fellow and tutor of Lincoln College, Oxford, since November 1729, he led the small society nicknamed the Holy Club or Methodists, which had been visiting prisoners in Oxford since August 1730. According to the Bicentennial editor, he refined the draft with advice from others, including his brother Charles and the Rector of Lincoln, Euseby Isham.

Missionary and minister at Savannah, Georgia, where he had arrived with his brother Charles aboard the Simmonds in February 1736, having embarked in October 1735. His father Samuel had died at Epworth in April 1735, shortly before he left England.

Back in England since landing at Deal on 1 February 1738 after the Georgia mission, and still a fellow of Lincoln College, he gave this less than three weeks after the Aldersgate Street meeting of 24 May 1738, where he recorded his heart 'strangely warmed'. The Bicentennial editor notes he had been barred from several pulpits while testing this message in London churches.

Working at Bristol, where on 2 April 1739, at George Whitefield's invitation, he had first preached in the open air, to about 3,000 people; the previous August he had visited the Moravians at Herrnhut. According to the Bicentennial editor, this sermon marked a breach with Whitefield that was never more than partly healed.

Still a fellow of Lincoln College, he had been preaching in the open air since April 1739, with the New Room at Bristol and the Foundery in London as his bases. His Journal records a sermon on the same text at Charles Square, London, a month earlier; the Bicentennial editor says John Gambold had warned him that Oxford hearers were prejudiced against him.

Still a fellow of Lincoln College, he preached this two months after presiding at the first Methodist Conference at the Foundery, London (25 June 1744); the previous October a mob had seized him during the Wednesbury riots. His Journal that day supposed it was his last time preaching at St Mary's, and in 1781 he wrote that the University paid others to take his turn.

When it was published in 1746 he was based at the Foundery in London, presiding over the annual conferences begun in 1744 and travelling continually; it was the year he began publishing Sermons on Several Occasions. He had first preached on the text at Long Acre, London, on 28 May 1738, four days after his Aldersgate experience.

The thirteen discourses appeared in 1748–1750, while he was based at the Foundery in London, presiding over the annual conferences and travelling continually, including in Ireland from August 1747; he still held his Lincoln College fellowship. Benjamin Ingham's Journal, cited by the Bicentennial editor, records him going through the Sermon on the Mount with the ship's company on the 1735–36 voyage to Georgia.

Published in 1750, the year before he married Mary Vazeille (February 1751) and resigned his Lincoln College fellowship that June. He was based at the Foundery in London, presiding over the annual conferences and touring England, Wales and Ireland. According to the Bicentennial editor, he had preached on the text twice in the autumn of 1749.

Married to Mary Vazeille since 1751 and no longer a fellow of Lincoln College, he was travelling continually on preaching tours that by now included Ireland and Scotland. His Journal records that he withdrew to Lewisham on 27 February 1758 to write the sermon, and that afterwards he declined the judge's invitation to dine because he had to set out.

Published in 1760 in the fourth volume of Sermons on Several Occasions, while he was based at the Foundery in London and travelling through England, Wales, Ireland and Scotland; he had been married since 1751. In January 1752 he, Charles and eleven colleagues signed a compact against passing on ill reports about one another; the Bicentennial editor records at least nine sermons against evil-speaking that year.

Published in 1760 as the sermon that completed the four volumes of Sermons on Several Occasions begun in 1746. He was then based at the Foundery in London, presiding over the annual conferences and travelling through England, Wales, Ireland and Scotland, and had been married to Mary Vazeille since 1751.

Published in 1765, while he was based at the Foundery in London, presiding over the annual conferences and travelling through England, Wales, Ireland and Scotland; he had been married to Mary Vazeille since 1751. The Bicentennial editor places it after his controversy with followers of Robert Sandeman over faith and assurance, at a time of unsettled views among the Methodists.

Based at the Foundery in London and presiding over the annual Methodist Conference, he was engaged on 10 November 1770 by Whitefield's friend Mr Keen, who, according to John Gillies, had repeatedly heard Whitefield name Wesley for the task. The Bicentennial editor notes that three months earlier Wesley's Conference had warned against leaning toward Calvinism, and that the breach over 'Free Grace' (1739) had never fully healed.

Living in the house beside City Road Chapel, his London headquarters since November 1778, he dated this text six weeks after ordaining Richard Whatcoat and Thomas Vasey for America at Bristol and setting apart Thomas Coke as superintendent. On 28 February 1784 he had executed the Deed of Declaration, legally defining the Methodist Conference. His estranged wife Mary had died in October 1781.

Living in the house beside City Road Chapel in London, he was away from the capital when, according to the Bicentennial editor, he finished this text at Wakefield on the morning of 1 May 1786 before leaving for Leeds. Two years earlier he had executed the Deed of Declaration, legally securing the Conference, and ordained preachers for America.

Based at City Road Chapel in London and living in the adjoining house, he dated this text at Manchester. It came three years after the Deed of Declaration legally secured the Conference and he ordained preachers for America, and six years after the death of his estranged wife Mary in October 1781.
